This study examines electron-electron interactions in graphene sheets at finite temperatures within the framework of the random phase approximation (RPA). We demonstrate that the graphene sheet supports a finite density of states at the Fermi level, even in the absence of external interactions. Our analysis reveals the persistence of massless Dirac fermions at nonzero energy scales and shows that the static longitudinal susceptibility remains divergence as the momentum approaches zero. We further establish that the dynamical susceptibility exhibits a low-frequency behavior characterized by a power law with an exponent of $2/3$. These theoretical predictions align closely with experimental observations of a nonzero specific heat coefficient at finite temperatures.

We introduce MaskedSpeech, a new strategy for generating speech context. The system employs a masking approach to create a more effective representation for the target context, which is provided as a text input. This method is straightforward to implement and can be integrated into various speech generation systems. We evaluated MaskedSpeech in the tasks of contextual and open-ended speech synthesis, demonstrating that it improves state-of-the-art results in both areas. The system's source code is publicly available at https://github.

We introduce a new method for distribution estimation that projects test samples onto the mean of the training data's support within a shared continuous latent space before applying mixture modeling to the resulting projected training data. This approach offers a streamlined framework that simplifies both training and inference while maintaining performance comparable to state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this strategy excels in scenarios where the test distribution is a subset of the training data, a situation frequently encountered in out-of-domain generalization and transfer learning.

Deep learning models are increasingly integrated into real-world applications, prompting a growing body of research into adversarial attacks that compromise their integrity. While prior work predominantly focuses on directly altering input data, this study introduces a novel attack vector wherein an adversary injects a covert, malicious generative model into the system. This malicious component operates in the background to produce data specifically engineered to cause misclassification. We demonstrate that this approach enables the development of attacks with lower error rates and greater sample efficiency compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical framework to analyze the capabilities and constraints of these assaults, culminating in suggestions for defensive strategies to mitigate the associated risks.

This research examines the social media activity surrounding climate change, with a specific focus on comparing the distribution of comments and network structures within Facebook groups dedicated to promoting versus refuting the phenomenon. We analyzed 1,100 Facebook groups, categorizing them based on their ideological alignment with the data, and subsequently extracted 11,000 profiles and 11,000 comments from 1,000 of these groups. Our analysis reveals that pro-climate change discourse is more prevalent in Facebook groups supporting the narrative, whereas skeptical posts dominate groups aligned with anti-climate change viewpoints. Furthermore, we observed that groups advocating against climate change exhibit higher connectivity and more intricate network structures compared to their supportive counterparts.

This study reports a search for dark matter produced alongside single top quarks or top quark pairs, utilizing proton-proton collision data from the CMS experiment at the LHC, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 137 fb$^{-1}$ collected at $\sqrt{s} =$ 13 TeV. The analysis examines final states containing one or two jets and one lepton (electron or muon), alongside various hadronic configurations. Dark matter candidates are inferred from significant missing transverse momentum. The observed event counts align with Standard Model predictions, a consistency that constrains simplified models of dark matter production in conjunction with top quarks. These limits are expressed as upper bounds on cross-sections across a range of mass combinations for the produced dark matter and top quarks.

This paper demonstrates that for a finite-dimensional algebra $\Lambda$, the $n$-extrangee structures on the derived category $\mathcal{D}^b(\text{mod-}\Lambda)$ satisfy Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality within the framework of $n$-exact derived categories, thereby establishing duality for $n$-extranged categories as seen in Serre duality.

This paper introduces a novel methodological framework for evaluating policy interventions that allow for multiple, simultaneous treatments in an unordered format. We establish new identification conditions that generalize the assumptions found in prior research on ordered multi-dimensional instruments, specifically by removing the necessity for monotonicity. Our theory is illustrated through an empirical analysis of the impact of undergraduate major selection on future labor market outcomes, utilizing data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1972. By leveraging the diverse array of available majors as an instrumental variable, we estimate the causal effect of choosing a specific major category. Our results indicate that these returns are substantially higher for science and engineering disciplines compared to other areas.

The Super $\psi$ factory, a proposed electron-positron collider, aims to scan the $J/\psi$ resonance with unprecedented precision in luminosity and energy resolution. Operating at the $J/\psi$ peak enables the production of these particles via the $e^+e^- \to J/\psi \to X$ process, where $X$ represents any hadronic final state. This mechanism facilitates the generation of exotic baryonic matter—including antineutrons and hyperons—in vast quantities. The paper demonstrates that the Super $\psi$ factory could produce $10^{10}$ antineutrons and $10^9$ of each charged hyperon species ($\Lambda$, $\Sigma$, and $\Xi$). These yields are sufficient to support high-precision measurements of fundamental properties such as magnetic and electric moments, as well as parity-violating interactions.

We have developed a numerical model to investigate accretion dynamics in hierarchical triple star systems that possess discs. Our simulations track the evolution of these systems from the initial phase of star and disc formation through to the final accretion stage. We examine how the disc mass and the initial configuration of the triple star system influence accretion outcomes. Our results indicate that the presence of a third star can either suppress or enhance accretion, depending on the specific system configuration.

We demonstrate that within the framework of lattice-based cosmology, the dynamics of the universe's expansion inherently lead to flat, Dyer-Roeder-type cosmological models. This conclusion arises from applying the Einstein equations to a dynamically evolving lattice representing a homogeneous yet anisotropic universe. In this model, the spatial metric is defined as $g_{ij} = a_i^2(t) \delta_{ij}$, where the direction-dependent scale factors $a_i$ evolve over time according to the function $a_i(t) = a_{i0} t^{2/3} [\Omega_{mi}/\Omega_{ci}]^{1/2}$, with $\Omega_{mi}$ and $\Omega_{ci}$ denoting the respective matter and curvature density parameters along the $i$-th axis. Although the global geometry remains anisotropic, the model exhibits inherent flatness because the sum of the individual density parameters across all dimensions satisfies $\sum_i (\Omega_{mi} + \Omega_{ci}) = 1$.

This paper introduces a new segmentation framework that couples image segmentation with various restoration processes. Unlike traditional methods, this approach utilizes a general framework for both segmentation and restoration, allowing the selection of any restoration model to achieve state-of-the-art results. The proposed method is applicable across diverse scenarios, including color segmentation, segmentation with boundaries, and the inclusion of regional constraints. Furthermore, it achieves significant improvements over existing techniques in color segmentation and boundary-aware tasks, as well as in region-constrained segmentation.

The observation of the event GW190521 by the LIGO/Virgo collaboration revealed a black hole with a mass located within the pair-instability gap, an anomaly that can be explained if the object is instead an ultralight bosonic body formed via the superradiant mechanism around a spinning black hole. This process generates compact objects with masses comparable to those observed, provided the bosonic field possesses a specific mass range. This paper investigates the observational signatures of such bosonic fields by analyzing the spins of massive black holes. Our findings indicate that the spin distribution of boson-formed black holes exhibits a pronounced peak at approximately 0.7, whereas those created through standard stellar evolution display a distribution peaking near 0.2. Applying this spin-distinguishing criterion to the catalog from the first O3 run of the LIGO/Virgo collaboration, we identified a significant excess of boson-formed candidates among O1 and O2 data, specifically finding a spin-distribution peak at 0.70 ± 0.15 for the boson-formed group versus 0.20 ± 0.10 for the stellar group. These results suggest a strong correlation between the two categories, yielding a statistical significance of 3.2σ.

Achieving rapid prototyping for Spiking Neural Network (SNN) algorithms on dedicated hardware like Intel Loihi is currently hindered by the necessity to convert models into specific formats compatible with the chip and transfer them physically. To address this, we introduce "brian2Loihi," a software solution that enables the direct execution of SNNs defined in Brian 2—a popular Python-based SNN framework—on the Loihi architecture. This tool operates as a hybrid utilizing Clyde, a C++ spike event engine, and a bespoke Brian 2-to-Loihi translator. The translator facilitates seamless model conversion from Brian 2 into a format Clyde can ingest, allowing the resulting executable to run on both the physical Loihi neuromorphic processor and the Clyde-emulated environment. This capability permits researchers to validate their SNN concepts on powerful general-purpose computing resources prior to deployment on physical hardware, thereby eliminating the need for physical model reformatting and sample submission. Furthermore, the system supports a "round-trip" workflow, where data collected from simulations can be reloaded to continue runs on either Clyde or Loihi. We demonstrate the utility of this framework by simulating a spiking classification task.

This study examines the magnetic field evolution of a microflare occurring in the solar quiet region, utilizing high-resolution spectroscopic data from the Solar Dynamics Observatory's Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) and the Solar and Heliospheric Mission's Spectrometer (SP). The analysis focuses on two noise storm sources situated in the same magnetic loop, revealing that their evolution is interconnected. Both events display a consistent decrease in Doppler shifts and an increase in Doppler broadening, indicating a reduction in upward flow velocity alongside heightened turbulence. Additionally, the source exhibiting the more intense noise storm exhibits a longer duration of flow deceleration, suggesting a stronger correlation between flow dynamics and the magnitude of the magnetic reconnection. The observed increase in noise storm intensity and broadening is attributed to heightened reconnection rates and the resulting acceleration of plasma within the loop. Furthermore, the extended deceleration period in the more active source supports the hypothesis that noise storm characteristics are linked to the initial pre-reconnection state of the magnetic field.

Atom-based sensors utilizing trapped atoms offer exceptional sensitivity for detecting electromagnetic fields, representing a significant advancement over traditional sensing methods. However, current systems rely on vacuum chambers that are bulky and difficult to integrate, restricting their application to large-scale infrastructure monitoring. This study introduces a novel compact magnetic optical trap (MOT) system, demonstrating the feasibility of a micro-scale setup with a chamber diameter of merely 3 cm. This breakthrough confirms the potential for widespread adoption of atom-based sensing technologies.

This study examines the accretion of a spherically symmetric, stationary, and self-gravitating gas cloud containing black holes, utilizing the relativistic Vlasov-Poisson system. The gas is characterized by a power-law distribution function, $f(E) = (E-E_0)^{-\alpha}$, where $E$ represents the specific energy, $E_0$ is a fixed reference energy, and $\alpha$ is a positive exponent. The analysis demonstrates that stationary solutions exist for all $\alpha > 0$ when $E_0=0$ and for $\alpha \in (0,2)$ when $E_0 \neq 0$. Furthermore, the study establishes the presence of angular momentum in these configurations. For the case of $E_0=0$, the maximum specific angular momentum scales as $L_{\rm max} \propto R^{\frac{2-\alpha}{2}}$, where $R$ denotes the cloud's finite radius. Conversely, for $E_0 \neq 0$, it scales as $L_{\rm max} \propto R^{\frac{1}{2}}$. The work also proves the stability of these solutions under axisymmetric perturbations, thereby extending prior one-dimensional stability results.

This study examines an atom interacting with a metallic mirror to investigate how atomic properties are modified by quantum vacuum fluctuations of the electromagnetic field. Specifically, the research analyzes how the atomic electric dipole moment is influenced by the motion of the mirror. The findings indicate that a mirror in motion induces a time-varying dipole moment, which serves as a source of electromagnetic radiation. The study further demonstrates that this radiative effect intensifies as a mirror approaches atomic scale dimensions and its velocity increases. Additionally, the work establishes a correspondence between this radiative mechanism and energy exchange resulting from a change in a atom's excitation state due to mirror movement, thereby linking it to the concept of work performed on the system.

We present the findings of a comprehensive study on the massive star population within the young cluster Westerlund 2, utilizing *Gaia* DR2 data to identify 1,000 sources with effective temperatures exceeding 10,000 K. By analyzing their *UBVJ* photometry and *Spitzer* infrared photometry and colors, we identified 100 objects likely to be protostars or stellar outflows. After removing these sources and applying decontamination techniques, we isolated a sample of 800 massive stars. We then constructed a color-magnitude diagram and a Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, which were used to determine the stars' evolutionary status. Our analysis indicates that the vast majority of the remaining population are still contracting pre-main-sequence stars. We also examined the spatial distribution of these objects, revealing a clear central concentration that aligns with predictions from Monte Carlo simulations. Finally, we estimated the cluster's total mass to be $7.5 \times 10^5 M_{\odot}$ and its age to be $3.5$ Myr.

This work examines a normalized solution for a specific type of fourth-order Choquard equation. By leveraging concentration-compactness principles alongside the Constrained Minimization Method, we establish the existence of a normalized ground state. A key distinguishing feature of this study is its inclusion of exponential non-linearities that grow essentially, a feature not commonly addressed in similar research.

Handwritten document restoration involves two core components: enhancing image quality and recognizing the written content. Although current research predominantly concentrates on the recognition aspect, often neglecting the initial image enhancement, this study addresses both tasks concurrently using a multi-task approach. We introduce a novel Multi-task Generative Adversarial Network (MT-GAN) designed to restore degraded handwritten texts by integrating two adversarial networks. The first network, a Multi-task Convolutional Network (MT-CONV), functions as the generator to produce restored images. The second, a Multi-disciplinary Discriminative Network (MD-Disc), acts as the generator to discriminate between authentic originals and artificially restored ones. By employing a joint training strategy, the system learns to generate high-quality reconstructions of degraded handwriting. Experimental results demonstrate that this method achieves state-of-the-art performance in handwriting recognition while delivering superior image restoration capabilities compared to existing solutions.

The proliferation of Optical Character Recognition (OCR) has significantly streamlined data entry by automarily extracting information from documents. This study introduces a novel approach for parsing Indonesian National Identity Cards, a process critical for transferring cardholder data to databases. The proposed system employs a two-stage extraction pipeline: first, OCR converts card text into machine-readable format, and second, Natural Language Processing (NLP) maps the recognized entities to their respective fields on the ID card. The NLP component utilizes a pre-trained Word2Vec model to enhance recognition accuracy. The paper concludes by detailing the experimental results and the performance metrics of this extraction framework.

This study introduces a novel time-averaging long short-term memory (TALSTM) scheme designed to enhance the performance of LSTM in assessing wireless channels. The primary objective is to achieve superior results with minimal channel state information (CSI) history, thereby reducing the computational burden associated with deep learning models. The proposed scheme is evaluated using data from the IEEE 802.11p standard, and its results are benchmarked against existing channel prediction techniques. The findings demonstrate that the TALSTM scheme outperforms other methods in terms of accuracy, computational efficiency, and overall effectiveness.

We introduce a methodology for astronomical image colorization and improvement utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). This approach involves two networks: a generator responsible for creating synthetic colors, and a discriminator tasked with evaluating their authenticity. We employed this framework to restore black-and-white Hubble Space Telescope images, successfully generating vibrant versions of the famous "Einstein Cross" and the "Whirlpool Galaxy."

Although neural networks are widely recognized for their ability to solve complex problems, their training typically relies on backpropagation, a method that requires calculating gradients. This reliance creates two significant drawbacks: first, it restricts their application to problems where gradients cannot be computed; second, the approximation errors inherent in gradient calculations can degrade solution quality. To address these limitations, this paper presents a novel, gradient-free architecture for solving both interpolation and classification tasks. The proposed method employs a sum of basis functions, with their parameters optimized via an iterative algorithm that avoids gradient computation. Validation through comparisons against benchmark problems demonstrates that this new structure achieves comparable accuracy to standard backpropagation-trained networks while remaining effective for tasks lacking differentiable gradients.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's Committee (ECFA-ECYR) was established in 2021 to foster a collaborative network for young professionals within the European Confederation for Fish Agglutinins Association. Comprising members at the postdoctoral level and below (including students), the committee focuses on advancing their research careers through strategic initiatives. Key activities include organizing regular meetings to discuss relevant topics, coordinating participation in ECFA conferences, and establishing regional subcommittees across Europe to strengthen local engagement and collaboration.

This study introduces a dual-surface metasurface system designed to control the generation of linear ripples. By employing a reflective and a transmissive metasurface, linear-to-line ripple conversion is realized, allowing for the manipulation of the ripples' polarization, propagation direction, and the orientation of the resulting lines. The proposed device offers a compact solution for polarization-to-ripple conversion, making it well-suited for optical imaging and sensing applications.

This study introduces a framework for scalable, distributed, and open cognitive AI architectures designed to facilitate large-scale learning in multi-agent systems involving humans and robots. This framework supports complex scenarios within extensive environments populated by numerous agents. We outline a distributed system that enables the simultaneous execution of multiple learning episodes across human-robot interactions, utilizing a cognitive architecture capable of managing distributed multi-agent dynamics. This system is built upon a distributed, scalable, and flexible infrastructure that supports various robot types, human participants, and interaction contexts. We present the system's design and implementation, demonstrating its efficacy through pilot tests in a large-scale setting where the infrastructure successfully coordinated learning tasks across 12 distinct human-robot dyads.

This study introduces an initial estimator for the population mean absolute deviation (MAD) about the median based on the sample MAD, utilizing a bias-correction technique. The initial estimator exhibits first-order consistency and asymptotic normality, with its bias diminishing at a rate of $O(n^{-1})$. A theoretical framework for the bias-correction step is established, and the proposed estimator demonstrates superior performance compared to the basic version in both simulation studies and real-world applications.

Relation extraction (RE) aims to identify relational pairs connecting a subject and an object within the textual span of an input sentence. Although recent advancements in RE have predominantly relied on neural architectures, a persistent issue involves incorrectly inferring relations between entity pairs that do not exist in established knowledge bases. This study addresses this limitation by integrating knowledge bases into the RE framework through a novel approach: jointly training a relation extractor and a knowledge graph link predictor on both textual sentences and knowledge graph data. By sharing representations between these models, we enable the link predictor to refine the extractor's output, thereby enhancing accuracy. Empirical results demonstrate that this joint training methodology surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques in both overall extraction performance and the precision of predicted relationships.

This study investigates quarkonium melting within a momentum-anisotropic QCD medium, incorporating the finite baryonic chemical potential. We calculate the quasi-particle Debye mass and subsequently derive the potential, self-energy, and screening mass for a hot medium exhibiting momentum anisotropy. Using these results, we analyze the quarkonium dissociation in an N-dimensional space, focusing on the impact of the chemical potential and anisotropic momentum on the melting behavior of various quarkonium states. Our results indicate that the chemical potential and momentum anisotropy significantly alter the dissociation characteristics of the medium. Specifically, increasing the quasi-particle Debye mass leads to a rise in the mass of the ground and excited states of quarkonium, thereby delaying their melting.

We report on the magnetic properties of Tb3RuO7, a rare-earth ruthenate characterized by alternating antiferromagnetic interactions within the Ru-O-Ru framework. Neutron diffraction data indicate that the Ru sublattice exhibits a long-range antiferromagnetic order below a critical temperature of $T_{\rm{N}} = 10.5$ K, involving a transition from a dimerized ground state to an alternating-chain structure. The observed magnetic behavior of the Tb sublattice aligns with theoretical predictions for a long-range antiferromagnetic chain featuring alternating single-ion anisotropy. Notably, the Tb3RuO7 system displays a unique partially disordered state at low temperatures, where the Tb sublattice remains dynamically disordered down to 1 K despite the Ru sublattice being statically ordered. This phenomenon is attributed to the Ru sublattice's internal nonuniform magnetic field, which suppresses Tb ordering through the rare effect of disordering by a static internal field.

This study examines the periodic activation patterns in deep neural networks (NNs) when processing images with varying spatial frequencies. We demonstrate that while standard random noise textures are commonly used to visualize specific neuron activations, these produce only a limited and unstable set of images. Consequently, we introduce images constructed from modulated sinusoidal carrier waves as a superior alternative for representation. These new images maintain consistency across frequencies and exhibit greater diversity. Furthermore, we demonstrate their utility by showing that neurons in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) respond to them with localized Gabor filters, whereas functional filters in fully connected layers are best described as two-dimensional Gabor filters with spatially varying properties.

Covariate shift occurs when the distribution of input features changes between the training and deployment environments, potentially compromising model performance. While traditional approaches like importance weighting or retraining address this issue, they often fail to account for data collected post-training that includes shifts in causal structure. This paper introduces semi-generative modeling, a framework designed to handle both covariate shift and structural causal changes. The method utilizes a semi-generative likelihood to jointly estimate causal relationships and probability distributions from pre- and post-deployment datasets. By integrating these learned components, the model constructs a covariate shift adjustment distribution used to reweight training samples. Experiments across synthetic benchmarks and real-world applications demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms baseline techniques, particularly in scenarios involving shifts in causal mechanisms.

Deep learning stands as a cornerstone of contemporary artificial intelligence, renowned for its capacity to excel in intricate tasks like image and speech recognition. This paper explores the geometric underpinnings of deep learning, revealing that the exceptional performance of the leading algorithms stems from the intrinsic geometric properties of their loss landscapes. We demonstrate that the training process of prominent models like convolutional neural networks (CNNs) inherently shapes these landscapes, causing them to resemble the convex regions found in highly over-parameterized statistical models. This similarity ensures that the loss surfaces of deep learning algorithms are amenable to optimization via standard gradient descent methods. Furthermore, we show that the transition from convexity to non-convexity in these landscapes is pivotal for achieving superior performance, as the specific geometric nature of the data dictates the resulting properties of the landscape and, consequently, the efficacy of the trained model.

We examine the relationship between main factors and the smallness of $|ζ(-1)|$, which is crucial for understanding why the energy per site in the main antiferromagnetic models is typically close to $-1$. This analysis reveals that the energy's proximity to $-1$ stems from the combined effects of the main factors, which can be unified under the concept of "lattice minima." Specifically, we show that when the Fourier transform of the interaction is minimized at the wave vectors corresponding to a particular lattice structure, the function $|ζ(-1)|$ attains a minimum. This minimization explains the energy term near $-1$ through the reduction of $|ζ(-1)|$.

This study applies Layerwise Relevance Propagation (LRP) to investigate deep neural network (DNN) jet taggers designed to distinguish prompt jets from jets containing decayed heavy-flavor quarks or leptons. The analysis focuses on two primary objectives: first, determining the relative significance of input variables within the model, and second, examining how these variables interact to influence the jet tagger's output. To achieve this, we introduce a set of "expert" variables that encapsulate established jet substructure techniques, contrasting them against the complex, often opaque inputs typical of standard taggers. Our findings reveal that these expert variables collectively account for over 90% of the DNN's decisions, with individual relevance scores mirroring their known physical and empirical utility in the field. Furthermore, we observe that the model leverages correlations among these experts to enhance performance, a capability that enables it to surpass standard jet taggers relying on intricate, non-interpretable features.

This paper introduces r-related degenerate Stirling numbers of the first and second kinds. These numbers allow for the expression in terms of r-related degenerate falling and rising factorials, generalizing the properties of the usual Stirling numbers. The study establishes identities connecting these numbers, including a formula for the convolution of r-related degenerate Stirling numbers of the first kind, along with the derivation of their respective triangular arrays and triangular array identities. Additionally, the authors derive explicit formulas for the triangular arrays, determine the relations between r-related degenerate and standard Stirling numbers, and demonstrate how the r-related degenerate factorial relates to the r-related power function. The work concludes with the identification of relations among the associated r-related degenerate exponential functions.

We examine the irreducible representations of strata groups, specifically focusing on the role of site and element symmetries in defining these representations. Our analysis covers both ordinary and strata groups, including the distinct cases of strata groups with inversion symmetry (ordinary) and those without (gray). We establish a correspondence linking the site symmetry group's representation theory to that of the resulting strata group, utilizing this framework to derive explicit irreducible representations for various irreps of the strata group.

We examine the application of Killing vector fields, whose associated flow lines are geodesics, to define Hermitian momentum operators that fulfill the fundamental commutation relations within an irreducible finite-dimensional irreducible representation of the Heisenberg algebra. This study occurs within the framework of Riemannian geometry on a connected manifold $M$ with dimension $n \geq 3$, where the underlying structure is a symmetric space of the non-symmetric type, specifically $M = G/K$. In this setting, $G$ denotes a connected simple Lie group, and $K$ is a maximal compact subgroup.

The Hubbard model serves as a fundamental framework for investigating strongly correlated electron systems, yet it is hindered by the sign problem, a challenge that severely limits Monte Carlo simulations to small system sizes and long timescales. While approximate functional theory and variational Monte Carlo offer potential alternatives, they often fail to capture sign-changing wavefunctions accurately, leading to incorrect physical predictions. This study introduces a neural network architecture designed to approximate the wavefunction of the Hubbard model; however, it mitigates the associated sign issue by leveraging the network's complex outputs instead of relying on a real-valued sign-magnitude formulation.

We examine a class of composite models wherein the Higgs boson emerges as a bound state of two scalar fields, termed flavons, which originate from the breaking scale of an $SU(3)_F$ flavour symmetry. This framework offers a unified solution to the issues of electroweak symmetry breaking and fermion mass hierarchies. We establish the conditions under which the Higgs potential remains stable and derive the resulting mass spectrum for both scalars and the associated KK excitations. Furthermore, we determine the production cross-sections and decay channels for the ground state flavons and their corresponding Kaluza-Klein towers, utilizing current experimental data from the LHC to derive constraints on the model's parameters.

Immersive technologies, such as virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR), have the potential to transform numerous sectors, yet their widespread adoption is hindered by the lack of consensus on ideal display standards. Perceptual distortions observed in these systems offer a pathway to establishing such benchmarks, as they provide measurable indicators of how users experience the digital world. This paper introduces a novel framework for investigating distortions in immersive systems, centered on a new methodology that utilizes the interaction between perceptual anomalies and the human desire for a consistent spatial understanding. By leveraging these insights, researchers can quantify the magnitude of visual discrepancies, thereby enabling more accurate predictions regarding their impact on perceptual experiences beyond immersion, specifically within areas like motion sickness and depth perception.

The BigScience multilingual pretraining framework introduces a method for efficiently creating multilingual language models by adjusting existing ones. This approach is cost-effective, enabling the development of models that reach 90% of the performance of dedicated alternatives with just 1/20th the cost and 1/40th the time. Although designed for established languages with substantial training data, this study investigates its applicability to understudied languages lacking extensive corpora. We evaluate the strategy using three understudied languages—Bambara, Breton, and Cherokee—demonstrating that the framework can be successfully applied to languages with limited available data.

We investigate the formation of binary systems during star formation, specifically focusing on the creation of a one-to-one mass ratio pair ($q=1$) with a total mass of $M_{\rm tot}=1\,M_\odot$ originating from a rotating, uniform-density, centrally condensed, parent core. By incrementally increasing the parent core's mass, we track the evolution of the system and identify the critical mass threshold where the central region undergoes gravitational collapse. This collapse yields a central fragment and a surrounding satellite; however, the satellite initially exceeds the central fragment in mass. Consequently, the satellite becomes dynamically unstable and fragments further into two equal-mass components. This sequence results in a final configuration of three stars where the central fragment and the two newly formed fragments from the satellite combine to form a binary system with $q=1$. We demonstrate that the sum of the masses of this resulting pair exceeds $0.5$ times the mass of the original parent core. Furthermore, we examine how variations in the parent core's mass influence the masses of the final binary components.

We introduce a new method termed "Autonomous Component Analysis" (A.K.A. m-ar-K-Fast), designed to extract multiple non-orthogonal features from data. This approach builds upon the Non-Linear Kernel Feature Mapping (A.K.A. N-K-F) technique introduced in 2018, which was originally intended for single-feature extraction. Our extension allows the user to specify the number of desired independent components, denoted as m. The resulting features are both self-explanatory and statistically independent, making them highly effective for downstream machine learning applications. Our analysis demonstrates that this technique serves as a universal approximator capable of representing any continuous function within the space defined by m independent components. Furthermore, we provide theoretical convergence guarantees for the algorithm and establish its robustness against outliers.

This study establishes a connection between finite model theory and proof complexity by examining the graph properties decidable within choiceless polynomial time (CPT) and their link to the extended polynomial calculus (EPC). We demonstrate that any graph property belonging to CPT lies within the polynomial time projection of an extended polynomial calculus (ECP) proof system. Conversely, we show that a specific logarithmic-size family of bipartite graphs can be distinguished in logarithmic depth choiceless tree semidistributions exactly when there exist ECP refutations of logarithmic size for the bipartite graphs' theories. These findings provide the first evidence suggesting a connection between non-logical choiceless computation and ECP proof complexity, hinting at a CPT-to-ECP analogue similar to the known link between PTIME and propositional resolution.

We introduce a novel infinite family of $\sigma$-elementary rings possessing an infinite, countable domain, with the specific property that their isomorphism classes are in one-to-one correspondence with the set of positive integers ($\mathbb{N}_{\ge 1}$).

Claims that cannot be refuted are ubiquitous in social media, where they frequently incite hostility and conflict. This study examines the structure of unfalsifiable claims within political discussions on Twitter involving Donald Trump and Barack Obama. Our analysis reveals that such claims predominantly originate from the periphery of social networks characterized by intense hostility. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the semantic landscape of unfalsifiable statements is tightly clustered around specific political figures, indicating a strong reliance on speaker identity. To address the dissemination of these statements, we propose a computational framework for identifying them and evaluate various strategies for alerting users to encounter these content.

Traffic incidents are a primary cause of congestion, resulting in significant economic losses. While various detection methods exist, this paper introduces a novel approach utilizing geotagged social media data to identify traffic incidents in real-time. By leveraging the ubiquity of smartphones and the tendency of drivers to post updates during incidents, this method offers a cost-effective alternative to traditional systems reliant on in-road sensors or cameras. We propose a new algorithm for analyzing tweet data that enables the rapid, real-time detection of incidents by efficiently identifying spatio-temporal patterns. Extensive testing on real-world datasets confirms the system's high accuracy and superior performance in real-time processing compared to existing methods.

We introduce a swift technique for calculating the CMB lensing-skewing bispectrum, which serves as a probe of primordial non-Gaussianity. This approach leverages the fact that the CMB lensing convergence $C_l$ and temperature anisotropies $T_l$ bispectra are effectively identical, allowing us to bypass the computationally expensive generation of full-sky lensed temperature maps. Instead, we compute the trispectrum of the underlying unlensed CMB directly, applying the "sky-skewing" method to derive the corresponding results for lensing convergence. We demonstrate that this strategy yields the $f_{\rm NG}$ bias term for the $CC\Delta$ configuration with a relative error of less than 10% across all multipoles, a precision sufficient for current observational capabilities. Furthermore, we show that the $CC\Delta$ skewness bispectrum is intrinsically linked to the cross-correlation between lensing convergence and CMB E-mode polarization ($EE$), suggesting that the skewness of this relationship offers an independent test of the Planck-determined $f_{\rm NG}$ bias.

Recent research has demonstrated that standard deep learning models can be circumvented by carefully crafted adversarial examples. While various strategies exist to enhance model robustness against such attacks, there is currently no method to verify this resilience at the inference stage. To address this gap, we introduce a new approach that integrates the concept of adversarial robustness into a Bayesian inference framework. By employing a hybrid inference mechanism, we enable the execution of Bayesian inference on trained models. Our method effectively captures uncertainty inherent in the training data and leverages this insight to guide the inference process. We validate the effectiveness of this technique through experiments on image classification tasks using the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets.

In the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, the rapid dissemination of online rumors has intensified, causing significant harm to public well-being and social stability. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a novel framework for analyzing the propagation and impact of cyber rumors. This approach utilizes a newly defined influence metric and applies the "spread method" to model the expansion of online narratives. Furthermore, the study examines the relationship between rumor reach and the associated negative effects, offering valuable insights for mitigating the consequences of rumor spread during the pandemic.

This study evaluates how various subspace dimensionality reduction techniques affect the classification of hyperspectral imagery. Using the Indian Pines dataset, we assessed pixel-level accuracy across three distinct reduction methods: spectral, spectral-spatial, and spatial reductions applied to the spectral component. Our analysis demonstrates that spectral dimensionality reduction can degrade classification accuracy, whereas applying reduction methods specifically designed for the spectral-spatial relationship yields superior results.

Language models are increasingly being compressed using modern compression techniques to facilitate deployment on devices with restricted memory. This study evaluates the compression rates of various popular LMs, including GPT-2, RoBERTa, and BERT, while also assessing compression fidelity. Our findings indicate that existing methods fail to preserve the generative capabilities of these language models effectively. To address this limitation, we introduce a new approach that combines quantization with a generative knowledge distillation framework. Experimental results demonstrate that this method achieves superior language reconstruction and generation capabilities compared to current state-of-the-art techniques.

We present a method for evaluating and refining protein structures by calculating amide proton ($^1$H$_{NH}$) chemical shifts through quantum mechanics (QM). This approach addresses the long-standing difficulty of experimentally resolving these shifts in isolated proteins, a hurdle that has previously hindered precise structural determination. By employingQM to simulate short peptides that mirror the local secondary structure of each residue, we can accurately predict the missing experimental data. Our results demonstrate that calculated shifts strongly correlate with experimental measurements ($R^2 = 0.94$) and are sensitive enough to distinguish between different hydrogen-bonding environments, such as those found in $\alpha$-helices versus $\beta$-sheets. We further show that incorporating QM-computed amide proton shifts significantly enhances the accuracy of protein backbones, resulting in improved agreement with nuclear Overhauser effect (NOE) distance restraints and better stereochemical properties.

Designing effective loss functions is essential for optimizing any model through gradient descent. This study investigates how different forms of a loss function influence the generalization capabilities of deep neural networks in classification tasks. We evaluate various architectures, including convolutional and recurrent networks, across image and text classification problems. Our findings indicate that while the specific choice of loss function does not drastically alter generalization performance, it significantly impacts the optimization trajectory.

We establish a connection between parquet theory and many-body perturbation theory within an expansion of the S-matrix, governed by a specific Hamiltonian that incorporates both parquet and counterterm operators as its components. This Hamiltonian yields a systematic series of S-matrix coefficients, which can be rigorously demonstrated to align exactly with those obtained through traditional parquet theory.

The phase transition observed in TiSe$_2$ to an excitonic insulator state is investigated using a *ab initio* approach. By modeling the system as a collection of excitons, we developed a first-principles framework based on the Landau theory of phase transitions. This theory employs the electron-hole susceptibility, which is computed via the $GW$ approximation alongside a two-particle self-consistent method. Our findings reveal that exciton condensation in this system stems from the coupling between charge density wave (CDW) and phonons, a mechanism that suppresses the CDG transition temperature.

Ensuring public safety is a critical priority for cities, and this study focuses on enabling effective communication between community members and municipal authorities. We investigate the U.S. "Safe Streets" initiative, a city-wide platform designed to accept safety-related reports. Our research examines the behaviors of both the general public and city dispatchers within this system. By analyzing the temporal dynamics of their exchanges, we uncover a pattern of "response delay," wherein dispatchers frequently take a considerable amount of time to address citizen submissions. Furthermore, we identify that certain dispatchers exhibit a tendency to prioritize reports based on their own interests rather than adhering strictly to a strict submission order. These discoveries offer valuable insights for enhancing dispatcher training and refining the operational protocols of reporting infrastructures aimed at ensuring equitable citizen service.

We examine a two-dimensional nematic superconductor, a state defined by gapless nodal quasiparticles and a nematic ordering that breaks rotational symmetry. Our analysis reveals that triplet Cooper pairs, which carry a spin aligned with an applied magnetic field, form anisotropic Fermi surfaces. This geometry generates a distinctive contribution to the magnetic susceptibility, arising from the differing radii of the Fermi surfaces along their major and minor axes. We calculate the resulting susceptibility and identify a crossover from behavior at low fields to that at higher fields.

Engaged learning represents a paradigm where a learner acquires knowledge through learning and subsequent engagement with tasks. This work formalizes engaged learning as a minimax differential game, wherein the learner employs a policy to regulate system engagement, while both a learning algorithm and an environment adversary seek to exploit any vulnerabilities within that policy. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, the learner can adopt a robust strategy capable of withstanding adversarial attacks. Furthermore, we outline a framework for modeling the environment adversary and detail methods for representing the resulting minimax differential game in discrete state spaces.

This study examines the informational complexity of Western music spanning 150 years (1870–2020) by analyzing 11,200 publicly available scores. We introduce a novel metric based on the conditional Kolmogorov complexity of musical pitch sequences, enhanced with a human-musician evaluation to ensure perceptual relevance. Our findings reveal a steady rise in average sequence complexity over this period. Specifically, music from the 1970s exhibits an average of 0.3 bits higher complexity per note compared to that from the 1870s, and music from the 1920s averages 0.2 bits more than music from the 1870s.

We examine a discrete-time reinforcement process featuring multiple entries, which generalizes the well-known Pólya urn model. In this framework, the system's state is defined by a countable set of non-negative integers, and the transition mechanism is determined by a countable matrix of probabilities. The process commences from a single entry at any specified initial state, with subsequent paths formed by sequences of states where the first path begins at the start node and every following path originates at the terminus of the prior one. The central objective is to determine the long-term behavior of this system. The analysis yields a countable stochastic matrix that fully characterizes the process, demonstrating that its asymptotic distribution aligns with a specific probability measure on the natural numbers. Furthermore, the study addresses the scenario where the process is launched simultaneously from every possible state. The findings reveal that the cumulative mass of such a process grows exponentially, with an exponent defined by the largest eigenvalue of the derived transition matrix.
