We introduce a novel approach to 2D/3D Hypergraph Visual Servoing (HVS) reconstruction, a technique capable of creating both structured and unstructured 3D models from multiple 2D point cloud views containing sparse features. Our method explicitly models the inter-view correspondences of these features as a hypergraph, where cameras act as nodes and feature points form the edges connecting them. By integrating sparse feature tracking with HVS, we simultaneously refine the poses of the views and the 3D positions of the features through sparse optimization. This process iterates until convergence, effectively rebuilding the scene's geometry and the camera trajectory. Furthermore, we employ a guidance strategy that leverages known 6-DoF poses to accelerate convergence and enhance the accuracy of the recovered 3D structure. Experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm successfully reconstructs complex environments, including those with significant motion blur and visual clutter, from sequences containing sparse features.

Medical imaging serves as a primary diagnostic tool in clinical practice, yet interpreting these images demands specialized expertise. Although radiologists are essential for accurate analysis, there is a pressing need to develop automated systems capable of analyzing images to support diagnosis and treatment planning. Current methods for extracting insights from images, however, often fail to align with actual radiological reasoning. This study introduces a novel, cost-effective, and precise technique for creating image annotations by utilizing CT projection. We applied this method to generate high-quality training data for a chest X-ray (CXR) dataset comprising over 100,000 instances. Furthermore, we established a new benchmark dataset, PA-CT, consisting of paired posterior-anterior CT and corresponding CT-projected CXR images, which facilitates the study of structural and semantic alignment between modalities. Finally, we proposed a new architecture, CT-AlignNet, designed to enhance the interpretation of CXRs by leveraging information from CT scans.

We establish a relationship between the Euler characteristic of minimal thurbon norm surfaces and the Thurstion norm of contact open book decompositions. As a result, we derive constraints on the Thurstion norm for certain contact Thurston norm divisors, demonstrating that specific such divisors cannot exist for tight contact structures on some 3-manifolds.

We introduce an entropy-based framework designed to characterize the spectral entropy per mode in microcavity lasers, offering a means to quantify the degree of unimodal emission. This approach proves particularly effective for analyzing entropy in emission spectra that are not strictly Gaussian. We further demonstrate that this spectral entropy can be computed by analyzing the far-field pattern, making it a viable parameter for monitoring the stability of laser output.

This study examines whether cryptocurrencies maintain stable value while functioning as a medium of exchange, utilizing an error-correction framework to analyze Bitcoin, Ethereum, and their relationship with US dollars over the period from 2015 to 2022. The analysis reveals that cryptocurrency values are unstable in the long term, yet demonstrate significant short-term stability. Specifically, both cryptocurrencies exhibit rapid correction toward their long-term equilibrium within a single day. These findings suggest that although cryptocurrencies are unsuitable for long-term store-of-value purposes, their ability to quickly adjust to equilibrium indicates they possess the potential to serve effectively as a medium of exchange.

We present the first rigorous demonstration of the weak noise limit, connecting stochastic Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) dynamics to a completely integrable framework. By applying a transformation that maps a given KPZ solution to one with flat height profiles, we establish a one-to-one correspondence between integrable random processes and the generalized KPZ equation. This transformation relies on the inverse scattering method of the Zakharov-Shabat system, adapted for space-time dependent potentials. Our findings confirm that, under an appropriate scaling regime, a general initial condition evolves toward a universal height distribution independent of the specific integrable model chosen. Furthermore, we derive a closed non-linear partial differential equation governing the three-point correlation function, a critical component for characterizing the scaling behavior of the weak noise KPZ phase.

Compressible magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence is a prevalent feature of the solar wind, characterized by shocklets and current sheets that facilitate efficient heating of the plasma. However, the specific mechanisms governing the transition from ion scales to electron scales remain unclear. This study utilizes data from the Magnetospheric Multiscale (MMS) mission to examine the electron-scale properties of compressive turbulence in the solar wind. We observed that the solar wind exhibits a pronounced anisotropy at electron scales, with spectral breaks occurring perpendicular to the mean magnetic field. Furthermore, we identified a consistent spectral break at the ion gyroradius in electron temperature fluctuations, even in the absence of ion-scale fluctuations in magnetic field variance. The observed electron parallel temperature spectrum is well-modeled by a power law with a slope of -2.7, which aligns with predictions from kinetic simulations of compressive Alfvénic turbulence. Additionally, we detected a distinct spectral break at the ion kinetic Alfvén wave (KAW) frequency in electron temperature fluctuations, a signature also present in simulation data. These findings suggest that electron-scale compressive turbulence is governed by electron KAWs, with a governing dispersion relation that mirrors that of ion KAWs.

This study introduces a novel approach to producing isolated attosecond pulses at XUV and soft X-ray free-electron lasers (FELs) through the chirp-taper method. The research demonstrates that the proposed scheme achieves a significantly higher saturation level for pulse isolation compared to prior iterations. Additionally, the effectiveness of the technique is enhanced by employing a linac-based energy modulator to generate a variable-energy electron bunch, which enables precise control over the resulting attosecond pulse duration.

The Rayleigh-Taylor instability (RTI) is a fluid dynamics phenomenon where a heavy fluid accelerates upward into a lighter one, a process often studied through simulations and experiments. This study examines the generation of RTI within a channel flow characterized by viscosity and stratification, specifically focusing on the transition from a shear-dominated regime to a gravity-dominated one. We demonstrate that the in situ generation of this instability can be quantified using the Richardson number modified for finite amplitude effects, denoted as $\mathrm{Ri}_\mathrm{f}$. This research also explores the relationship between the growth rate of the instability and the shear wavenumber, noting that the most unstable mode exhibits a higher horizontal scale than the direct forcing wavenumber. Furthermore, we show that the maximum growth rate occurs at a lower value of $\mathrm{Ri}_\mathrm{f}$ than previously established in inviscid theories. These findings are significant because they expand the range of conditions under which physical optics models can reliably estimate the onset of shear-induced instabilities.

Gerrymandering remains a critical issue in the United States, where it manipulates electoral district boundaries to unfairly advantage a political party. Although the U.S. Supreme Court has recently established new standards for evaluating such redistricting practices, the fundamental question of how to quantify gerrymandering persists. This paper introduces a novel approach leveraging simulated annealing, a technique that effectively identifies the most egregious aspects of a districting plan by measuring how it distorts a party's vote share relative to its actual support. By optimizing the detection of manipulation, this algorithm proves highly versatile, functioning successfully across various map geometries and even nonspatial vote distributions. Furthermore, the methodology is capable of evaluating the fairness of existing legislative maps in the U.S. Congress.

Defect identification in textiles is a critical step in the patterned fabric printing workflow. This study introduces a new defect detection approach that integrates Gabor-HOG with matrix completion techniques. Initially, Local Binary Patterns (LBP) and Gabor-HOG features are extracted from image blocks to characterize visual properties. Subsequently, these features are arranged into a feature matrix, where low-rank decomposition is applied to separate the matrix into a primary structure component and a sparse residual. The latter isolates specific anomalies, including flaws and voids. Finally, defect regions are delineated through morphological processing and centroid calculation. Experimental outcomes indicate that this methodology achieves a 96.1% detection rate and a 95.1% false alarm rate, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing techniques.

This work introduces a reinforcement learning approach for autonomous visual inspection, where a camera manipulator is controlled by a policy network to identify defects on product surfaces. To enhance the policy's ability to discover novel anomalies, we incorporate a regularization term into the reinforcement learning objective based on the mutual information between the selected viewpoints and the detected defects. This mutual information term serves as an exploration bonus that promotes active learning within the visual guidance process. Furthermore, we employ an efficient approximation of the mutual information utilizing the variational lower bound, which facilitates training using only single trajectories. Experimental evaluations on a high-speed printing press demonstrate that this proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques in an industrial inspection setting.

We establish a limit on the rate at which a black hole can shed mass through Bond accretion. This limit is determined by the black hole's ability to form an event horizon, which requires that the Bondi radius remain smaller than the black hole's apparent (or trapping) radius. This apparent radius is defined as the location where the inward pressure force exactly balances the outward force of gravity. We demonstrate that this condition imposes a strict upper bound on the Bondi mass loss rate, expressed as $\dot{M}_B \leqslant 4\pi c^3/G \cdot r_B^2$, where $r_B$ represents the Bondi radius. This maximum rate corresponds to the scenario in which the black hole's specific adiabatic gradient equals $4/3$. For an adiabatic index lower than $4/3$, the black hole cannot maintain a stable horizon because the Bondi mass loss rate would exceed this limit. We further show that this theoretical upper bound aligns with the Bondi accretion rate calculated at the apparent radius.

We investigate the gravitational wave luminosity generated by merging white dwarfs (WDs) within nuclear star clusters (NSCs), which typically host massive black holes capable of consuming the surrounding population of stars. Our findings indicate that in galaxies hosting NSCs with masses exceeding $10^5$ solar masses, the WD merger rate surpasses $10^{-1}$ Gpc$^{-1}$ yr$^{-1}$. This level of activity could potentially allow current detectors to identify individual events, offering a novel method to probe the properties of NSCs and their resident white dwarfs.

The escalating frequency of disturbances affecting power delivery systems stems from a convergence of factors, including the aging infrastructure, deteriorating equipment, and the intensification of severe weather events. These incidents degrade the overall quality of power supplied to end consumers. While incident detection and subsequent restoration represent the cornerstone of reliable energy delivery, traditional methods often rely on human operators interpreting visual cues from SCADA systems or analyzing voltage and current waveforms. This human-centric approach is increasingly untenable given the rapid expansion of grid assets and the intensifying workload on staff. Consequently, this paper advocates for a paradigm shift toward data-driven methodologies for incident identification. We outline a strategy to detect faults within distribution networks by leveraging monitoring data from smart meters, a method designed to remain robust against anomalies in the data. Furthermore, we employ classification models to pinpoint incidents specifically within later stages of the network, utilizing boundary condition information from aggregate substation transformers.

Text-based games offer an engaging framework for assessing language models' abilities in reasoning, planning, and problem-solving. However, existing game environments suffer from performance bottlenecks, processing game steps too slowly to enable large-scale exploration. We introduce TextWorldExpress, a high-performance version of the TextWorld problem space that executes game actions up to 100 times faster than the original. This system is built on the Mimalloc-enhanced A* search algorithm, optimized C++ code, and the MPMock graphics library. TextWorldExpress enables the exploration of 200 times more states within the same timeframe compared to the standard version. This performance leap facilitates the discovery of previously unknown problems and allows for efficient, large-scale reinforcement learning experiments. Ultimately, this speed makes it feasible to collect over 1 billion trajectories per day, significantly advancing progress toward creating more capable automated agents.

This study introduces a mathematical framework for topological insulators (TIs) that inherently supports defects. In this approach, the TI's electronic structure is defined by a Hermitian operator on a Hilbert space, with its topology determined by the kernel of a nearby regular operator. By leveraging the existing kernel and its associated eigenspaces, the model naturally accommodates the TI's electronic properties alongside various defects.

This paper examines the Dirichlet problem for $p$-harmonic functions within a planar sector. By leveraging the Liouville–Green transformation, the problem is reformulated in terms of a second-order linear differential equation. The study derives explicit formulas for the Dirichlet eigenfunctions and eigenvalues, alongside positive $p$-harmonic functions expressed via power and trigonometric powers. Furthermore, the paper provides a general solution for the Dirichlet problem and investigates the regularity of these solutions.

This work introduces a new multivariate distribution designed to model the spatial conditionally extreme sea surface, encompassing significant wave height and peak wave period. The proposed framework relies on a standard Gaussian copula paired with a univariate spatial extremal model for the significant wave height. Peak wave period is subsequently modeled as a function of significant wave height, utilizing a log-linear relationship with spatially varying coefficients. The validity of this approach is confirmed through its successful application to reanalysis data spanning the North Atlantic and the North and Baltic Seas.

This work establishes the following theorem: For a fixed field $K$ and integers $g_1, g_2, g_2 \geq 1$, there exists a positive integer $N$ such that for any non-constant separable maps $\phi$ from a smooth, projective, non-hyperelliptic curve $C_1$ of genus $g_1$ to a smooth, projective curve $C_2$ of genus $g_2$ over $K$, the condition $\deg \phi \geq N$ implies that $g_1 = g_2 = g$. This paper also addresses several related inquiries.

Manipulation capability is a fundamental aspect of robot performance, yet it varies significantly based on the specific configuration. To address this, we introduce a method for estimating a robot's manipulability by leveraging human manipulability data. Our approach involves learning a manipulability model that maps the human joint angles to the robot's joint positions, effectively transforming the robot's domain into the human's. This transformation addresses the inherent nonlinearity of robotic kinematics through a manifold-aware Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm enhanced by parallel transport. We evaluate this model across various scenarios, including different human populations, body sizes, and species of robots, demonstrating strong performance.

This study examines the sensitivity of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) to detecting the non-standard production of two Higgs bosons decaying into $b\bar{b}$ and $WW^*$ final states. The analysis employs matrix element techniques to isolate signal events from the dominant backgrounds, specifically $t\bar{t}H$ production and the irreducible component of vector boson fusion. The study concludes that the High-Luminosity LHC can achieve a 95% confidence level sensitivity to cross-section enhancements of approximately 2.5 times the Standard Model prediction.

We introduce a novel 3D object recognition strategy that relies on a specific prior: the assumption that a 3D object's pose is unintentionally encoded in the image by the act of the object rotating. This assumption is realized through an end-to-end trainable network designed to identify a 3D pose from a single image. This inferred pose is then mapped to a reference view through a 3D render, where the loss function optimizes the match between the input image and the rendered appearance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that this method achieves state-of-the-art performance in 3D object recognition using only a single image.

This study examines the propagation of misinformation regarding COVID-19 vaccines on Twitter, with a specific focus on identifying the underlying motivations behind its sharing. By leveraging the CoToNa-CoV dataset, which contains over 100,000 English tweets accompanied by human-annotated sharing intentions (either acceptance or rejection), the research introduces an advanced fine-tuning approach for BERT-based models. These techniques were employed to develop classifiers capable of accurately distinguishing between acceptance and rejection intents. The proposed method achieved an F1-score of 0.809, surpassing the performance of state-of-the-art models by a significant margin of 0.111 in F1-score.

The interaction of intense infrared fields with krypton gas yields a train of isolated attosecond pulses, a phenomenon that enables the direct observation of electron dynamics on the sub-cycle scale. This study demonstrates the capability to modulate the intensity of a single attosecond pulse within this train by varying the intensity of an additional infrared field. This modification results in a 20-fold variation in pulse intensity, corresponding to a change of 12 orders of magnitude. This discovery marks a significant advancement in the field of high-harmonic generation, offering a novel approach to the strong-field control of coherent radiation.

The eclipsing binary Algol (Beta Persei) has been extensively studied for over a century, with its primary star being eclipsed by a secondary component every 2.867 days. While historical data from the 19th and early 20th centuries hinted at a third body, the discovery of the eclipsing eclipsing variable V358 Persei in 1998 was initially interpreted as this third object. However, subsequent research established that V358 Persei is merely an unrelated background binary system. This study utilizes high-precision photometry from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) to investigate the Algol system. The analysis reveals a new periodicity of 1.015 days, represented by a shallow dip of 0.003 magnitudes. Although this feature was previously detected in ground-based data, its exact nature remained ambiguous. We propose that this signal originates from Algol's primary star, driven by the gravitational influence of a fourth body. Modeling the event as a grazing transit suggests the candidate companion has a mass of 0.0011 ± 0.0002 solar masses, corresponding to a radius of 0.012 ± 0.001 solar radii. This candidate represents the tightest-orbiting companion ever identified around Algol, with a semi-major axis of 0.0041 ± 0.00

We examine the time-dependent nonlinear Schrödinger equation within the domain outside a fixed obstacle in $\mathbb{R}^d$ (for $d \geq 3$), subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions. The equation's nonlinearity is of the focusing type, $|u|^{p-1}u$, with the exponent constrained by $1 < p < \frac{d+2}{d-2}$ for dimensions $d \geq 3$ and any exponent for $d=1,2$. The initial data $\psi_0$ is assumed to reside in the Sobolev space $H^1_0(\Omega)$, where $\Omega$ denotes the obstacle's exterior. Our analysis demonstrates that if the initial energy is strictly below the ground state threshold and the $L^2$-norm of the initial data exceeds that of a ground state solution, the corresponding solution exhibits blow-up behavior within a finite time.

Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have proven effective for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) across various fields, yet they face significant hurdles when applied to high-dimensional PDEs or those with intricate geometries. Specifically, the excessive computational cost associated with PINNs in these contexts often necessitates the use of approximate solvers, which can degrade solution accuracy. Furthermore, the standard PINN framework relies on a fixed uniform node set, meaning initial node distribution critically influences both the quality of the outcome and the required computational resources. This paper introduces Residual-based Adaptive Node Generation (RANG), a technique designed to mitigate these drawbacks by dynamically adding nodes in regions of high error to enhance solution precision while lowering overall computational load. Additionally, RANG offers greater adaptability by allowing users to define custom solution metrics through a residual function, unlike the standard mean-squared error loss function. Validated against several benchmark PDEs, the RANG method demonstrates superior accuracy and efficiency compared to the conventional PINN approach. The corresponding open-source code is available at https://github.com/zhengy99/RANG-PINN.

This study introduces a novel adverse capacitance phenomenon in multi-domain ferroelectric FETs, arising from the alignment of polarization vectors parallel to the channel. The physical mechanisms driving this effect are elucidated, and the analysis demonstrates that the magnitude of the resulting charge accumulation is contingent upon the distance between domains. Furthermore, the adverse capacitance exerts a significant influence on the electrostatic control of the channel, thereby modulating the device's switching characteristics. The paper concludes by presenting an analytical framework for characterizing the properties of this unique capacitance and its impact on the I-V and C-V profiles of FeFETs.

The cargo ecosystem encompasses a complex web of interconnected entities, including shippers, shipping lines, ports, and cargo agents, whose interactions are governed by various contractual agreements. This intricate network renders the entire system susceptible to disruptions originating from the failure of a single entity or link. To address this, we introduce a Dependency-Weakness Knowledge Graph (DW-KG) designed to map both cargo ecosystem entities and their relationships, while explicitly modeling the specific dependencies and weakness attributes of each participant. Utilizing advanced Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques, we developed an automated approach for constructing this knowledge graph. Furthermore, we employed network analysis methods to evaluate the vulnerability propagation mechanisms within the cargo network. The findings demonstrate that our proposed methodology effectively uncovers the latent dependency and weakness characteristics inherent within cargo ecosystem documents.

This study examines a class of stochastic Ginzburg-Landau equations influenced by pure jump noise and driven by Lévy space. We establish the existence of a unique ergodic measure, demonstrating both the existence of a unique stationary distribution and the system's irreducibility. Furthermore, by leveraging these findings, we derive a explicit form of the invariant density for the group. As a direct application, we investigate the long-term behavior of the system's energy.

This paper presents an explicit formula for the minimum order of the reduced power graph $\mathrm{RP}(G)$ when $G$ is a finite nilpotent group, alongside a complete characterization of those power graph orders that are prime. The study also identifies the specific elements of $\mathrm{R}\mathrm{P}(G)$ with maximal and minimal distances, providing the resulting distance diameter for the graph. Furthermore, it determines the exact conditions under which the power graph $\mathrm{P}(G)$ is isomorphic to the distance graph $\mathrm{D}_2(G)$, the cycle graph $C_N$, or is a complete graph $K_N$.

This document outlines the design of a proposed hadron spectrometer intended for the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The instrument aims to investigate hadron structure and interactions by measuring differential cross-sections for proton-proton scattering across a wide range of momentum transfers ($t$) and center-of-mass energies. It is specifically designed to detect final states involving protons and neutrons with low transverse momenta ($p_T < 1$ GeV/c) up to a maximum $|t|$ of 0.5 GeV$^2/c^2$, extending its reach to the highest possible luminosity. The system will also precisely determine the kinematics of events containing forward heavy ions, enabling the study of hadron production within such collisions. Additionally, it will analyze hadron production triggered by cosmic rays exceeding an energy threshold of 10$^{17}$ eV.

This study introduces Directional Convolutional Networks (DCNs), a new framework for image recognition. The model employs directional filters to capture both local and global image structures, effectively addressing the limitations of standard convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in mastering long-range spatial dependencies. The approach is straightforward, utilizing an architecture that mirrors conventional CNNs but replaces standard kernels with directional filters. The methodology is highly efficient, requiring minimal computational overhead compared to conventional models. The paper presents the full methodology, including a new filter design, training procedures, and inference mechanisms. Empirical evaluations on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets demonstrate that DCNs achieve significant performance gains over baseline CNNs, delivering higher accuracy with fewer parameters and reduced training time.

Point clouds serve as a prevalent 3D representation, yet Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have not historically been the primary choice for processing this format. This paper introduces a methodology for applying GCNs to point cloud data, demonstrating that with specific modifications, these networks can effectively handle such inputs. We present a comprehensive analysis of key design choices, illustrating how each influences performance. Our findings offer valuable insights for future research aimed at applying GCNs to point cloud handling.

The paper introduces a novel semantic trojan attack that targets code-obscuring techniques such as obfuscation and control-flow integrity (CFI). Unlike traditional methods which insert standard logic gates as functionals, this approach adds minimal, arbitrary signal disruptions to alter computation outcomes without establishing new stable states. Consequently, the trojan payload remains undetectable by tools that scan for host functionality or semantic anomalies. Although the resulting modifications are functionally nonsensical, their effects can be engineered to produce specific, desired behaviors. We developed an automated framework capable of identifying, synthesizing, and verifying these host-less trojans, successfully validating their efficacy against various levels of protection including no defense, code obfuscation, and CFI.

The Magellan Imaging and Spectrograph (IMACS) at Las Campanas Observatory has been adapted to host the Remotely Operable Spectrograph for IMACS (ROSIE). ROSIE is an integral field spectrograph (IFS) designed to deliver high-resolution spectra across a 1.2 arcmin x 1.2 arcmin field of view. It achieves this by utilizing a 256 x 256 Hamamatsu multianode microchannel plate detector, which offers high quantum efficiency and rapid readout speeds. This detector captures light from a 2D micromirror array positioned at the Cassegrain focus, where each individual mirror functions as a spatially resolved slit. These micro-reflectors are fabricated using standard photolithography techniques on a silicon substrate and coated with a highly reflective gold layer. The system operates by directing the beam through a cross-disperser spectrograph equipped with a Hamamatsu MCP detector to record spectra for each illuminated micromirror. The development of ROSIE was driven by the need for a flexible IFS capable of supporting diverse scientific investigations, ranging from galactic archaeology to the study of exoplanets.

This study examines the current state of carbon-12 nucleus-nucleus fusion, a reaction pivotal to the carbon, neon, and oxygen burning stages in stellar evolution. We specifically address the issue of subbarrier fusion enhancement, which cannot be explained by conventional theories relying on the universal, short-range nuclear interaction alone. We propose that this enhancement arises from the coupling between the relative motion of the nuclei and their internal degrees of freedom, a mechanism analogous to the Trojan-horse effect observed in three-body systems. We further outline a novel experimental methodology utilizing a "nuclear Trojan-horse" to measure fusion cross-sections at energies below the Coulomb barrier, aiming to elucidate the underlying fusion enhancement mechanism.

We present high-resolution, high signal-to-noise ratio spectra for 100 planet-hosting stars, enabling the measurement of 12 elemental abundances (Fe, Mg, Si, Ca, Ti, Al, Mn, Ni, Cr, Na, K, and S) in 80 of them. Our analysis reveals that the observed scatter in stellar abundances is consistent with theoretical predictions regarding the formation of the Solar System and the chemical evolution of the Galaxy. These findings allow us to infer the compositions of the building blocks for terrestrial-type exoplanets, suggesting their bulk compositions are largely uniform. Consequently, we estimate the mass of the material stripped from such planets due to giant impacts to be less than 0.01% of the planet's total mass.

Current localization methods relying on channel state information (CSI) typically utilize neural networks to map received signals to locations. However, these approaches often fail to address the critical issue of feature redundancy. This study introduces localization attention, a mechanism designed to enhance the representational capability of CSI by selectively focusing on the most informative features. By employing a hierarchical encoder-decoder framework, attention is integrated into each layer to refine the learning process. Experimental evaluations across two distinct environments confirm the method's efficacy, demonstrating significant improvements in accuracy: 20.1% in an office setting and 14.5% in an auditorium, relative to standard CSI-based localization techniques.

We introduce a general framework for modal logics based on topological categories. This approach unifies and extends various topological and algebraic semantics found in both classical and intuitionistic modal logic. In this setting, the carrier objects represent possible worlds, while the morphisms connecting them function as the modal operators. We demonstrate the method's applicability by identifying the topology category, enriched topology categories, and functor categories as valid examples.

A graph $G$ admits a $k$-edge-coloring if its edges can be assigned one of $k$ colors such that no two adjacent edges share the same color. Within this context, a robust edge-coloring of $G$ is defined as a $k$-edge-coloring where every color class forms a matching. While it is established that a cubic bipartite graph $G$ with a maximum edge-matching size of $\alpha'(G)$ admits a 4-edge-coloring, this paper investigates the corresponding 4-edge-coloring for $G$. Specifically, we demonstrate that there exists a cubic bipartite graph $G$ for which every 4-edge-coloring fails to be a matching of size $\alpha'(G)$, thereby proving that a robust 4-edge-coloring is not always feasible.

This work presents new upper limits for real-valued functions defined on Hamming graphs, specifically targeting function classes with specified upper eigenvalues. For a function possessing an upper eigenvalue of $-1$, the bound corresponds to the count of distinct elements in the graph, while restricting the eigenvalue to a maximum of $1$ yields the bound of $2n$, where $n$ represents the graph's dimension. These findings extend and refine earlier outcomes by Godsil, which were limited to functions with eigenvalues not exceeding $0$ or $1$. Furthermore, the authors derive tight lower bounds for functions with minimum eigenvalues of $1$ or $3$; notably, the bound for functions with min eigenvalue $1$ encompasses all constant functions on the set $\{0,1\}$ with an average value of $1$.

COPASI is a highly capable simulation environment for biochemical networks, yet its desktop interface presents usability barriers for both general users and developers. To address this limitation, we introduce ShinyCOPASI, an intuitive web-based frontend that streamlines model exploration and result analysis. This platform supports interactive engagement with COPASI models via RESTful APIs, allowing users to modify simulation parameters, execute runs, and visualize outputs through dynamic graphs and tables. We have deployed ShinyCOPASI to host COPASI models submitted to BioModels, a major repository for these networks. This deployment enables users to access and investigate these models without local installation, while also facilitating the seamless integration of existing models into new research workflows.

This study presents an evaluation of various uncertainty quantification techniques for neural networks, specifically tailored for scientific machine learning applications. We assess multiple categories of uncertainty metrics, including Bayesian approaches, ensemble methods, and non-intrusive data-driven strategies, by testing them on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our analysis examines how these methods perform in terms of calibration, efficiency, and their ability to generalize, ultimately providing a comprehensive comparison to guide future research and practical deployment in physics-informed machine learning contexts.

This paper introduces a function algebra analogous to the one studied by Enock and Woods on a compact quantum group. We establish that for the newly defined algebra, the von Neumann algebra is a finite type II₁ factor. Additionally, we determine its trace and demonstrate that this algebras type (i.e., being a type II₁ factor) holds universally for all compact quantum groups.

This study introduces a novel algorithm for computing value function iterations in discrete-state Markov decision processes (MDPs) characterized by extensive dimensions. Leveraging the concept of imprecise probability theory, we propose a robust variant of GMRES policy iteration (IGMRES-PI). This method integrates GMRES into the fixed-value iterations of policy iteration by employing an ellipsoidal framework to manage uncertainty. The robust nature of IGMRES-PI allows it to mitigate the policy iteration phenomenon, a known limitation in traditional approaches. We present a theoretical analysis of the algorithm's convergence and demonstrate its efficacy through various numerical experiments.

Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a weighted oriented graph with edge ideal $I(\mathcal{D})$. This paper establishes a combinatorial criterion for determining when a monomial $x_{i}^{a_{i}} \cdots x_{j}^{a_{j}} \cdots x_{k}^{a_{k}}$ belongs to the $\mathbf{t}$-th power of this ideal, denoted as $[I(\mathcal{D})]^{\mathbf{t}}$, and likewise for the strong version $[I(\mathcal{D})]^{s\mathbf{t}}$. These characterizations are expressed using properties of the underlying undirected graph and the associated directed acyclic graph $\mathcal{D}$. As a direct consequence, we derive a formula for calculating the $\mathbf{t}$-th (and strongly $\mathbf{t}$-th) mixed volume of $\mathcal{D}$, denoted as $\mathbf{t}\text{-vol}(I(\mathcal{D}))$.

This study introduces a novel approach to the inverse problem for computer models producing time series data, aiming to identify the input that yields a specific output trajectory. We propose the Contour Estimation Method (CSM), which approximates the conditional density of inputs given observed series by sampling from the joint contour of the series' marginal densities. This work investigates the potential of incorporating local neighborhood information to enhance robustness in classification tasks. We introduce a learning framework where a model accesses limited neighborhood data around each input instance. Leveraging this locality information, we derive robust generalization bounds for several representative scenarios. These bounds facilitate the identification of optimal strategies for leveraging neighborhood data and are utilized to propose several novel algorithms. We evaluate these methods across multiple datasets for both image and text classification tasks, demonstrating significant robust performance gains over current state-of-the-art techniques.

This study examines how jet fragmentation evolves within the quark-gluon medium in Pb-Pb collisions, utilizing jets tagged by isolated photons to constrain the initial transverse momentum of the scattered parton. The analysis focuses on the medium's impact on the fragmentation function, specifically the high-$p_T$ hadron distribution relative to the photon. Comparing these results across centrality classes reveals a significant suppression of high-$p_T$ hadrons in the most central collisions, alongside an enhancement observed at lower $p_T$. These findings are compared against predictions from perturbative QCD calculations and models incorporating parton energy loss and hadronization effects.

In this paper, we establish several Apéry-type series featuring mixed summation indices by employing an integral method. These series are expressed as linear combinations of colored multiple zeta functions (CMZFs) and their derivatives evaluated at 1, 1/2, and 1. Our findings extend the results presented in our earlier work [10].

This study presents the findings of a multi-wavelength investigation into the enigmatic brown dwarf WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, commonly referred to as "The Mishap." This object was initially identified as a candidate for the nearest isolated brown dwarf yet was later discovered to possess a complex, variable spectrum that defies standard classification. Our analysis reveals that its spectrum exhibits significant variability across multiple timescales, featuring prominent emission features in the H$\alpha$ line and broad molecular bands of CO and CN. Additionally, we observed a notable discrepancy between its optical and near-infrared colors and those predicted by current evolutionary models. These observations suggest the presence of a chromosphere and active magnetic phenomena, including flaring events. Collectively, these results indicate that this object's characteristics are more consistent with those of an active binary system than with an isolated brown dwarf.

This study reports the production yields of pions, kaons, (anti-)protons, and $\phi$ mesons in central Xe-Xe collisions at a center-of-mass energy per nucleon pair of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.44$ TeV. The data were collected by the ALICE experiment at the LHC using a $10\,\mathrm{mb}^{-1}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ luminosity. The results are compared with predictions from various models to investigate the formation of a quark-gluon plasma in heavy-ion collisions.

We introduce a novel method for parton distribution function (PDF) evolution and interpolation that leverages JIMWLK equations within the framework of effective (x-dependent) Lagrangians. This approach utilizes a basis of functions that are orthogonal under a weighted inner product, where the weight is defined by a specific PDF metric. The resulting effective Lagrangians generate a system of ordinary differential equations governing the expansion coefficients; solving this system yields both an evolved and reparametrized PDF. Numerical results demonstrate that this procedure maintains high precision, even at large x values, while simultaneously producing analytic expressions for PDF moments.

This study examines how sintering temperature influences the microstructure and mechanical properties of pressed pellets made from simulated lunar and Martian regolith. We evaluated the phase composition and microstructure of the pellets using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Additionally, we assessed mechanical strength through three-point bending tests and measured thermal conductivity via the laser flash method. Our findings indicate that increasing the sintering temperature promotes the formation of a glassy phase and enhances both mechanical strength and thermal conductivity. These results provide valuable insights for developing in-situ 3D printing technologies on Mars and the Moon.

This study examines the instability of a liquid film coating a cylindrical fiber, with a specific focus on how the nature of the solid-liquid interface slip influences the onset of Rayleigh-Plateau instability. By employing lubrication theory, we derive an amplitude evolution equation for the surface disturbances, which reveals that slip at the boundary amplifies the instability, resulting in shorter wavelengths and elevated growth rates. These theoretical predictions are corroborated by direct numerical simulations of the full Navier-Stokes equations. Furthermore, we observe a transition in the character of the flow within the liquid; it shifts from a laminar state to a chaotic regime marked by significant energy dissipation and the generation of vorticity.

This study utilizes the 200$\mu$m and 70$\mu$m data from the Herschel survey, alongside optical and near-infrared observations from the VLT, to investigate the relationship between star formation rates (SFR) in nearby galaxies and the Brackett-$\gamma$ (Br$\gamma$) line flux. We selected a sample of 100 galaxies with a mean redshift of 0.012, where Br$\gamma$ emission is clearly detectable and SFR values were derived using spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting. The resulting Br$\gamma$-based SFRs show a strong correlation with those obtained from SED fitting, yielding a correlation coefficient of 0.82. The average ratio between the Br$\gamma$ and SED-fitted SFRs is 0.92, with a scatter of 0.4 dex. This scatter is consistent with the combined uncertainties of both methods, indicating that Br$\gamma$ serves as a reliable standard for calibrating SFR estimates from SED fitting.

This article serves as the first installment in a two-part study dedicated to classifying unitary $\mathfrak{sl}_N$ subgroups within rational conformal field theories (RCFTs) characterized by a large level $k$. We concentrate specifically on type $II$ subgroups, which establish a one-to-one correspondence between the characters of the parent theory and regional modules of the subtype. These symmetries permit the construction of an extensive set of automorphisms acting on the regional module category; we analyze these explicitly for the case of $\mathfrak{sl}_N$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that such automorphisms are essentially limited to those already inherent to the theory. The conceptual framework developed here will be utilized in the following paper to achieve the overall classification.

This study introduces a new method for solving the differential equation $u_t = \Delta (|u|^{p-1}u)$, where $p>0$. The core component is a first-order finite difference scheme in time, which is unconditionally stable and exhibits $O(\Delta t)$ convergence. This scheme is implemented using an operator splitting technique that decomposes the diffusion term into $N$ sequential linear subproblems for an $N$-dimensional spatial domain. By applying the transformation $v = |u|^{(p-1)/2}u$, these subproblems transform into linear diffusion equations. The resulting systems are solved using the multigrid method, which offers both $O(N)$ memory efficiency and $O(N \log N)$ computational speed.

This paper introduces a novel methodology for recognizing handwritten mathematical expressions utilizing pen-based data. The study evaluates the performance of various machine learning models, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Long Short-Term Memory networks (LSTMs), and hybrid models, in classifying these expressions. The results indicate that the best outcomes were achieved by combining CNNs with a single-layer LSTM, which demonstrated an accuracy of 90.1%.

This study introduces a synthetic method for generating speech duration by integrating the median of multiple speech recognition systems. This technique offers a computationally efficient, non-parametric method that proves effective in generating a speech corpus for the development of duration models. This speech corpus is then used to train a speech duration model, which is then used to predict the speech duration of a new, unseen test set. This process is then repeated by integrating the median of multiple speech recognition systems.
